description: AeroDynamicX bridges aerospace engineering and immersive storytelling for NASA's 'Abandoned but not Forgotten.' We use mission datasets and creative digital modeling to bring the forgotten history of discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars to life. Our diverse team of engineers and data analysts is fully ready to innovate in the 2026 Space Apps Challenge!
summary: Many of NASA’s most famous spacecraft have finished their missions or gone quiet, and their stories end up scattered across archives. We built AeroDynamicX to put 30 of them in one place you can actually explore. You fly around a 3D solar system, from the Moon and Mars to the gas giants and interstellar space, and jump into any mission. You can take each spacecraft apart piece by piece, listen to its story, compare it with others, and test what you’ve learned with quizzes and a certification exam. We made it for students and space fans who want to learn how these machines work by playing with them.
details:
What it does: AeroDynamicX turns NASA mission data into something you can explore. The home screen is a live 3D map of the solar system with 30 missions grouped into six destinations. Every spacecraft has a 3D model you can pull apart to see its parts, specs and what each one contributed to the science. Each also has a narrated story, NASA images and a labeled parts view. Some craft even have a payload console where you can pilot the spacecraft and try its instruments.

Learning side: The Compare Dock lets you put up to three spacecraft next to each other and look at mass, speed, power, distance and lifespan. Each craft has a short quiz, and a perfect score earns XP and a collectible mission patch. There is also a 10-question certification exam across all destinations (70% to pass) that gives you a personalized PDF certificate.

Accessibility: We added a text mode and a low-graphics mode so it still works on slower devices and for people who can’t use the 3D view.

Why it matters: These missions took decades of work, and we didn’t want that to fade. This gives students a hands-on way to learn real spacecraft engineering.

How we built it: We designed the interface using our own knowledge together with Google design studio, and we pull NASA data through NASA’s API. [Add the languages and libraries you used, for example JavaScript and three.js, if that’s right.]

What makes it creative: We wanted it to feel like mission control, so learning works like moving up through a space program, with ranks, patches and a final certification.

What we considered: Getting the science right, keeping it fast on ordinary devices, making it accessible, and giving clear credit to every data source.
